claim: Focal cortical stroke in mouse forelimb motor cortex leads to a complete loss of neurons in all cortical layers of the illuminated hemisphere.
source: The procedure led to a complete loss of neurons in all cortical layers of the illuminated hemisphere (Figure 1a).
evidence: The claim is supported by histological data presented in Figure 1a showing Nissl staining of the lesion.

claim: The photothrombotic lesion was typically restricted to the gray matter.
source: The lesion was typically restricted to the gray matter (see Nissl staining in Figure 1a).
evidence: The claim is supported by Nissl staining data shown in Figure 1a.

claim: In about 25% of mice, partial damage was detected in the dorsal aspect of the white matter.
source: In a minority (about 25%) of the mice, partial damage was detected in the dorsal aspect of the white matter, as demonstrated by reduced staining for myelin basic protein (MBP; Figure 1a, inset).
evidence: The claim is supported by MBP staining data shown in Figure 1a inset.

claim: Single-pulse optogenetic stimulation evokes a field potential with an early negative wave peaking between 17 and 26 ms after stimulation.
source: In deep layers, single-pulse stimulation evoked a FP with two main components: (i) an early negative wave, peaking between 17 and 26 ms after stimulation
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1a.

claim: Single-pulse optogenetic stimulation evokes a field potential with a late positive component peaking between 40 and 60 ms.
source: In deep layers, single-pulse stimulation evoked a FP with two main components: (i) an early negative wave, peaking between 17 and 26 ms after stimulation and (ii) a late positive component, peaking between 40 and 60 ms (Figure 1—figure supplement 1a, black trace).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1a.

claim: The early negative-going field potential is due to direct transcallosal excitation.
source: Pharmacological dissection of the two components indicated that the early negative-going FP is due to direct transcallosal excitation, while the late positive peak corresponds to disynaptic inhibition of target neurons via local GABAergic cells (Restani et al., 2009; Palmer et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by pharmacological experiments and cited literature (Restani et al., 2009; Palmer et al., 2012).

claim: The late positive peak corresponds to disynaptic inhibition of target neurons via local GABAergic cells.
source: Pharmacological dissection of the two components indicated that the early negative-going FP is due to direct transcallosal excitation, while the late positive peak corresponds to disynaptic inhibition of target neurons via local GABAergic cells (Restani et al., 2009; Palmer et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by pharmacological experiments and cited literature (Restani et al., 2009; Palmer et al., 2012).

claim: Local delivery of the GABA-B antagonist CPG55845 had no significant effect on the negative-going field potential in naïve mice.
source: Indeed, local delivery over the cortex of the GABA-B antagonist CPG55845 in naïve mice had no significant effect on the negative-going FP (Figure 1—figure supplement 1a,b)
evidence: The claim is supported by pharmacological data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1a,b.

claim: Local delivery of CPG55845 substantially reduced the positive-going component of the field potential.
source: Indeed, local delivery over the cortex of the GABA-B antagonist CPG55845 in naïve mice had no significant effect on the negative-going FP (Figure 1—figure supplement 1a,b) but substantially reduced the positive-going component (Figure 1—figure supplement 1a,c), consistent for a role of GABA-B signaling in interhemispheric inhibition (Irlbacher et al., 2007; Palmer et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by pharmacological data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1a,c and cited literature (Irlbacher et al., 2007; Palmer et al., 2012).

claim: Topical application of CNQX completely abolished the field potential responses.
source: Topical application over the cortex of CNQX, a blocker of glutamatergic transmission, completely abolished the responses, confirming the post-synaptic origin of the recorded FPs (Figure 1—figure supplement 1a, blue trace).
evidence: The claim is supported by pharmacological data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1a.

claim: The amplitude of the negative field potential component was dramatically dampened in stroke animals at 5 days.
source: Analysis of the initial, negative component demonstrated that the FP amplitude was dramatically dampened in stroke animals at 5 days (two way ANOVA, followed by Holm-Sidak test, p<0.05; Figure 1d,e)
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 1d,e with statistical analysis.

claim: At 30 days after stroke, the main negative wave was partly reinstated but still significantly lower with respect to sham controls.
source: At 30 days after stroke, the main negative wave was partly reinstated, but still significantly lower with respect to sham controls (two way ANOVA, followed by Holm-Sidak test, p<0.05; Figure 1d,e).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 1d,e with statistical analysis.

claim: The late positive component showed greater amplitudes in stroke animals at 30 days, with difference maximized in the central-deep layers.
source: Quantification of the late positive component showed greater amplitudes in stroke animals at 30 days, with difference maximized in the central-deep layers (two way ANOVA, followed by Holm-Sidak test, p<0.05; Figure 1f).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 1f with statistical analysis.

claim: There is an imbalance in interhemispheric connectivity early after stroke, with weaker direct excitation but paradoxical enhancement of transcallosally mediated inhibition.
source: Altogether these data demonstrate an imbalance in interhemispheric connectivity early after stroke, with weaker direct excitation but paradoxical enhancement of transcallosally mediated inhibition.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the electrophysiological data presented in Figure 1.

claim: The amplitude of the field potential response progressively increased with light intensity in both healthy and stroke mice.
source: Determination of input/output curves (i.e. amplitude of the negative-going FP vs. intensity of stimulation) established that the amplitude of the response progressively increased with light intensity in both healthy and stroke mice.
evidence: The claim is supported by input/output curve data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1d.

claim: The responses of ischemic animals were scaled down and reached saturation earlier than healthy mice.
source: However, the responses of ischemic animals were scaled down and reached saturation earlier (n = 5 Stroke and n = 5 Sham animals, two way ANOVA, followed by Tukey test, p<0.05; Figure 1—figure supplement 1d).
evidence: The claim is supported by input/output curve data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1d with statistical analysis.

claim: Current source density analysis revealed a main current sink spanning all cortical layers with the shortest latency in infragranular layers.
source: The analysis revealed a main current sink (red) spanning all cortical layers and with the shortest latency in infragranular layers.
evidence: The claim is supported by CSD analysis shown in Figure 2a.

claim: Initial current sinks were followed by sources which were particularly prominent in the deep layers of the ipsilesional RFA.
source: These initial current sinks were followed by sources (blue) which were particularly prominent in the deep layers of the ipsilesional RFA.
evidence: The claim is supported by CSD analysis shown in Figure 2a.

claim: The current sinks were consistently dampened in the RFA of ischemic animals at 30 days.
source: The current sinks were consistently dampened in the RFA of ischemic animals at 30 days (Figure 2a)
evidence: The claim is supported by CSD analysis shown in Figure 2a.

claim: Stimulus-evoked multi-unit activity was substantially reduced in stroke mice compared to control mice.
source: The analysis revealed robust stimulus-evoked response at a depth corresponding mainly to cortical layer V in control mice (Figure 2b, top). This activity was substantially reduced in stroke mice (Figure 2b, bottom).
evidence: The claim is supported by MUA data shown in Figure 2b.

claim: The negative and positive components of the evoked field potential were always higher and lower, respectively, in the contralesional RFA than in the perilesional RFA of individual stroke mice.
source: In particular, the negative and positive components were always higher and lower, respectively, in the contralesional RFA than in the perilesional RFA of individual stroke mice (Figure 2d,e; paired T test, negative component p=0.003 and positive component p=0.012).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 2d,e with statistical analysis.

claim: In naïve controls, the amplitude of the two field potential components was comparable in the two hemispheres.
source: In naïve controls, the amplitude of the two FP components was comparable in the two hemispheres (Figure 2d,e; paired T test, negative component p=1 and positive component p=0.06).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 2d,e with statistical analysis.

claim: The robust asymmetry between the field potential response recorded in the ipsilesional and contralesional cortex after transcallosal stimulation suggests that the alterations in interhemispheric communication are caused by plastic rearrangements after stroke and not by direct callosal damage.
source: The robust asymmetry between the FP response recorded in the ipsilesional and contralesional cortex after transcallosal stimulation suggests that the alterations in interhemispheric communication are caused by plastic rearrangements after stroke and not by direct callosal damage.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation based on the asymmetry data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Local delivery of the GABA-B antagonist CPG55845 potently reduced the positive-going field potential 30 days after stroke.
source: As expected, local delivery over the cortex of the GABA-B antagonist CPG55845 potently reduced the positive-going FP 30 days after stroke (Figure 3a,b)
evidence: The claim is supported by pharmacological data shown in Figure 3a,b.

claim: The Paired Pulse Ratio was significantly lower in stroke animals with respect to controls.
source: The PPR was significantly lower in stroke animals with respect to controls, consistent with enhanced transcallosal inhibition in ischemic vs. sham animals (Figure 3d).
evidence: The claim is supported by paired-pulse data shown in Figure 3d.

claim: The Paired Pulse Ratio was significantly lower in middle-deep layers of stroke animals.
source: In particular, the PPR was significantly lower in middle-deep layers of stroke animals (T test, p<0.05).
evidence: The claim is supported by MUA paired-pulse analysis shown in Figure 3e with statistical analysis.

claim: SNAP-25 cleavage was evident along all cortical layers and spanned the entire CFA after BoNT/E injection.
source: We found that SNAP-25 cleavage was evident along all cortical layers and spanned the entire CFA.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Cleaved SNAP-25 persisted for at least 10 days after BoNT/E injection.
source: Western Blot analysis indicated persistence of cleaved SNAP-25 for at least 10 days after injection (Figure 4g).
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 4g.

claim: Unilateral BoNT/E injection in naïve mice showed a transient deficit in performance of the contralateral forelimb, which was significant on day two post-injection.
source: Behavioral analysis of motor function in naïve mice (n = 5) injected unilaterally with BoNT/E showed a transient deficit in performance of the contralateral forelimb (evaluated with Gridwalk and Schallert Cylinder tests), which was significant on day two post-injection (two way RM ANOVA followed by Tukey test, Day 2 Gridwalk p=0.014, Schallert p=0.03; Figure 4—figure supplement 1a,b)
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1a,b with statistical analysis.

claim: Performance returned to baseline on day 9 after BoNT/E injection and remained stable up to 30 days post-injection.
source: Performance returned to baseline on day 9 (Gridwalk p=0.251 and Schallert p=0.781) and remained stable up to 30 days post-injection (Figure 4—figure supplement 1a,b).
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1a,b with statistical analysis.

claim: Silencing of the healthy hemisphere led to functional gains in the Gridwalk test.
source: As shown in Figure 4h, the silencing of the healthy hemisphere led to functional gains in the Gridwalk test but was completely ineffective in the Schallert Cylinder task.
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 4h.

claim: Silencing of the healthy hemisphere was completely ineffective in the Schallert Cylinder task.
source: As shown in Figure 4h, the silencing of the healthy hemisphere led to functional gains in the Gridwalk test but was completely ineffective in the Schallert Cylinder task.
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 4h.

claim: In the Gridwalk test, the BoNT/E-treated group was superior to untreated stroke at several time points (day 9, 16, and 23).
source: In the Gridwalk test, the BoNT/E-treated group was superior to untreated stroke at several time points (two way RM ANOVA followed by Tukey test, day 9 p=0.05, day 16 p=0.002, day 23 p=0.001).
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 4h with statistical analysis.

claim: At 30 days, the BoNT group was not distinguishable from untreated stroke in the Gridwalk test.
source: However, at 30 days the BoNT group was not distinguishable from untreated stroke (p=0.094).
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data with statistical analysis.

claim: Daily robotic training induced an improvement in the parameters related to the retraction task on the M-Platform.
source: Consistent with previous results (Spalletti et al., 2014), the daily robotic training induced an improvement in the parameters related to the retraction task on the M-Platform (Figure 6—figure supplement 1a,b).
evidence: The claim is supported by robotic platform data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1a,b and cited literature (Spalletti et al., 2014).

claim: Robotic training improvement was not generalized to other forelimb tasks, as demonstrated by the lack of recovery in Schallert and Gridwalk tests.
source: However, we found that this improvement was not generalized to other forelimb task, as demonstrated by the lack of recovery in Schallert and Gridwalk tests, where the motor deficit remained stable over the observation period (Figure 6a,b).
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 6a,b.

claim: Robot+BoNT mice showed significant improvements in both Gridwalk and Schallert Cylinder tests, especially at day 30.
source: In both tests, Robot+BoNT mice showed significant improvements, especially at day 30 (two way repeated measures ANOVA followed by Tukey test, Robot+BoNT vs Robot, Gridwalk p<0.001, Schallert p<0.05).
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 6a,b with statistical analysis.

claim: Performances in Robot+BoNT group remained improved at 40 days with respect to animals undergoing only robotic rehabilitation.
source: We found that performances in Robot+BoNT group remained improved at 40 days with respect to animals undergoing only robotic rehabilitation (two way repeated measures ANOVA, Robot vs. Robot+BoNT 40 days, p<0.05) (Figure 6c,d).
evidence: The claim is supported by follow-up behavioral data shown in Figure 6c,d with statistical analysis.

claim: No differences between 30 and 40 days time points were found for both Robot and Robot+BoNT groups.
source: Of note, no differences between 30 and 40 days time points were found for both groups.
evidence: The claim is supported by follow-up behavioral data analysis.

claim: In the Gridwalk test, Robot+BoNT group was superior to Robot and untreated stroke groups.
source: In the Gridwalk test, Robot+BoNT (n = 11) group was superior to Robot (n = 10) and untreated stroke (one way ANOVA followed by Tukey test p<0.001), but statistically comparable to BoNT/E only (p=0.45).
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 7a with statistical analysis.

claim: In the Schallert cylinder test, mice receiving the combined therapy displayed markedly improved performances with respect to all the other groups.
source: In the Schallert cylinder test, mice receiving the combined therapy displayed markedly improved performances with respect to all the other groups (one way ANOVA followed by Tukey test, p=0.023 vs BoNT, p=0.005 vs stroke untreated and p=0.01 vs Robot).
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 7b with statistical analysis.

claim: The percentage of errors in the Single Pellet Retrieval task increased 2 days after stroke but was recovered in the animals with combined therapy at 16 days and remained stable at 30 days.
source: We found that the percentage of errors in the Single Pellet Retrieval task increased 2 days after stroke but was recovered in the animals with combined therapy at 16 days and remained stable at 30 days (Two way RM ANOVA followed by Tukey test vs Baseline, p=0.55 at day 16 and p=0.989 at day 30; Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by skilled reaching data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1 with statistical analysis.

claim: Recovery of prehension was significantly more robust in the Robot+BoNT group as compared to untreated stroke.
source: Recovery of prehension was significantly more robust in the Robot+BoNT group as compared to untreated stroke (p<0.01; Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by skilled reaching data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1 with statistical analysis.

claim: The total length of the trajectory (ArcLen) appeared to recover at day 23 post lesion in Robot+BoNT group.
source: In particular, the total length of the trajectory (ArcLen) appeared to recover at day 23 post lesion in Robot+BoNT group (Figure 8b, two way ANOVA followed by Tukey's test vs Baseline, p=0.08).
evidence: The claim is supported by kinematic data shown in Figure 8b with statistical analysis.

claim: A significant improvement was reported at day 30 for the total area spanned by the trajectory (AUC).
source: A significant improvement was also reported at day 30 for the total area spanned by the trajectory (AUC) (Figure 8c, p=0.49).
evidence: The claim is supported by kinematic data shown in Figure 8c with statistical analysis.

claim: A significant restoration of pre-lesion values was detected for the mean speed and for the smoothness of the reaching movement.
source: Of note, a significant restoration of pre-lesion values was also detected for the mean speed and for the smoothness of the reaching movement (Figure 8e and f, p=0.31 at day 16 and p=0.17 at Day 30 for Mean Speed and Smoothness respectively).
evidence: The claim is supported by kinematic data shown in Figure 8e,f with statistical analysis.

claim: ArcLen, AUC and mean speed measured at 30 days in the Robot+BoNT group were significantly different from the untreated stroke group.
source: ArcLen, AUC and mean speed measured at 30 days in the Robot+BoNT group were also significantly different from the untreated stroke group (two way repeated measures ANOVA followed by Tukey test, p<0.001).
evidence: The claim is supported by kinematic data with statistical analysis.

claim: Differences between the treated and control animals were not due to different extent of lesion, as the deficits on day two were equivalent and the ischemic volumes were superimposable between the groups.
source: Differences between the treated and control animals were not due to different extent of lesion, as the deficits on day two were equivalent (Figure 8) and the ischemic volumes were superimposable between the groups (T test p=0.702, Figure 8—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by lesion volume data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 2 with statistical analysis.

claim: The density of PV+ cells were decreased after stroke with respect to sham condition.
source: We found that the density of PV+ cells were decreased after stroke (n = 8) with respect to sham condition (n = 7,T test, p<0.001).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemical data with statistical analysis.

claim: The Robot+BoNT treatment further accentuated the decline in PV+ cells and the number was significantly lower with respect to untreated stroke.
source: The Robot+BoNT treatment further accentuated this decline and the number of PV+ cells was significantly lower with respect to untreated stroke (n = 6, Figure 9a,b; T test, p=0.045).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemical data shown in Figure 9a,b with statistical analysis.

claim: The number of SOM+ cells is significantly lower after stroke with respect to sham.
source: The number of these cells is significantly lower after stroke with respect to sham (n = 6 sham and n = 4 stroke untreated; T test, p<0.001)
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemical data with statistical analysis.

claim: In the rehabilitated group, the number of SOM+ cells was even more diminished compared to untreated stroke.
source: but in the rehabilitated group was even more diminished (n = 6; Figure 9c,d; T test, p=0.014).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemical data shown in Figure 9c,d with statistical analysis.

claim: A significant MBP decrease was found in the combined treatment group.
source: We found a significant MBP decrease in the combined treatment group (Figure 9e,f; T test, p=0.045)
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemical data shown in Figure 9e,f with statistical analysis.

claim: The early negative component of the field potential was not rescued in the Robot+BoNT mice and only partly recovered in deep layers.
source: Both the CSD and the LFP quantification show that the early negative component of the FP (reflecting direct transcallosal excitation) was not rescued in the Robot+BoNT mice and only partly recovered in deep layers (two way ANOVA followed by Tukey's test p=0.089, Figure 10b,c).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 10b,c with statistical analysis.

claim: The late positive component was almost completely normalized in the combined therapy group.
source: However, the late positive component (indicating transcallosal, GABA-B mediated inhibition; see Figure 3a,b) was almost completely normalized in the combined therapy group.
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 10.

claim: The amplitude of the positive-going field potential was significantly reduced with respect to untreated stroke in superficial/middle and middle/deep layers.
source: In particular, the amplitude of the positive-going FP was significantly reduced with respect to untreated stroke in superficial/middle and middle/deep layers (two way ANOVA followed by Tukey's test, p=0.009).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 10d with statistical analysis.

claim: The positive-going field potential was comparable to sham animals across all the cortical layers in the Robot+BoNT group.
source: Moreover, it was comparable to sham animals across all the cortical layers (Figure 10b,d).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 10b,d.

claim: The paired-pulse depression was rescued in Robot+BoNT mice in superficial/middle, middle/deep and deep layers.
source: In keeping with these data, also the PPD was rescued in Robot+BoNT mice in superficial/middle, middle/deep and deep layers, as shown from the PPD ratio of the field potential (two way ANOVA followed by Tukey's test, Robot+Bont vs Stroke untreated, p<0.01, Figure 10e).
evidence: The claim is supported by paired-pulse data shown in Figure 10e with statistical analysis.

claim: Robots represent a valid approach to increase the amount and repeatability of exercises in stroke rehabilitation.
source: In particular, robots represent a valid approach to increase the amount and repeatability of the exercises (Lo et al., 2010; Klamroth-Marganska et al., 2014; Reinkensmeyer et al., 2016)
evidence: The claim is supported by cited literature (Lo et al., 2010; Klamroth-Marganska et al., 2014; Reinkensmeyer et al., 2016).

claim: Robotic devices allow for highly standardized therapeutic protocols.
source: allowing for highly standardized therapeutic protocols (Loureiro et al., 2011)
evidence: The claim is supported by cited literature (Loureiro et al., 2011).

claim: Robotic devices have competitive costs compared to conventional therapy.
source: with competitive costs compared to conventional therapy (Wagner et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by cited literature (Wagner et al., 2011).

claim: Robotic devices collect objective and quantitative data about the performance of each patient, characterized by different kinetic and kinematic parameters.
source: Importantly, they collect objective and quantitative data about the performance of each patient, characterized by different kinetic and kinematic parameters (i.e. force exerted by the subject, smoothness of the movement, etc., Reinkensmeyer et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by cited literature (Reinkensmeyer et al., 2016).

claim: Physical rehabilitation should be combined with 'plasticity-stimulating' or neuromodulatory interventions that render the spared CNS networks more susceptible to experience-dependent modifications.
source: It is also increasingly recognized that physical rehabilitation should be combined with 'plasticity-stimulating' or neuromodulatory interventions that render the spared CNS networks more susceptible to experience-dependent modifications (Zeiler and Krakauer, 2013; Straudi et al., 2016; Tran et al., 2016; Alia et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by cited literature (Zeiler and Krakauer, 2013; Straudi et al., 2016; Tran et al., 2016; Alia et al., 2017).

claim: Plasticity in the injured hemisphere plays a major role in post-stroke motor recovery and is a primary target for rehabilitation therapy.
source: In this context, plasticity in the injured hemisphere plays a major role in post-stroke motor recovery and is a primary target for rehabilitation therapy.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge in the field.

claim: Stimulation of the ipsilesional motor cortex, especially when paired with motor training, facilitates plasticity and functional restoration.
source: Indeed stimulation of the ipsilesional motor cortex, especially when paired with motor training, facilitates plasticity and functional restoration (Allman et al., 2016; Dodd et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by cited literature (Allman et al., 2016; Dodd et al., 2017).

claim: The role of the contralesional hemisphere remains highly controversial.
source: On the other hand, the role of the contralesional hemisphere remains highly controversial (Dancause et al., 2015; Talelli et al., 2012; Buetefisch, 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by cited literature (Dancause et al., 2015; Talelli et al., 2012; Buetefisch, 2015).

claim: The interhemispheric competition model posits an enhanced transcallosal inhibition exerted by the healthy side over the spared perilesional tissue.
source: Attempts to promote stroke recovery by inhibiting the contralesional hemisphere are based on the interhemispheric competition model, which posits an enhanced transcallosal inhibition exerted by the healthy side over the spared perilesional tissue (Murase et al., 2004; Dancause et al., 2015; Barry et al., 2014; Silasi and Murphy, 2014; Boddington and Reynolds, 2017; Mansoori et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by cited literature (Murase et al., 2004; Dancause et al., 2015; Barry et al., 2014; Silasi and Murphy, 2014; Boddington and Reynolds, 2017; Mansoori et al., 2014).

claim: Direct electrophysiological measures of the evolution of interhemispheric inhibition post-stroke are not yet available.
source: However, direct electrophysiological measures of the evolution of interhemispheric inhibition post-stroke are not yet available.
evidence: The claim is a statement about the state of the field at the time of writing.

claim: Inactivation of the healthy hemisphere via either low-frequency, repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS) or cathodal (inhibitory) transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS) has yielded some positive yet variable effects in clinical trials.
source: Second, inactivation of the healthy hemisphere via either low-frequency, repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS) or cathodal (inhibitory) transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS) has yielded some positive yet variable effects in clinical trials (Kim et al., 2010; Lefaucheur et al., 2014; Di Pino et al., 2014; Plow et al., 2016; Volz et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by cited literature (Kim et al., 2010; Lefaucheur et al., 2014; Di Pino et al., 2014; Plow et al., 2016; Volz et al., 2017).

claim: Variability in outcome of contralesional hemisphere inactivation may depend on the extent of damage: interhemispheric competition dominates in patients with limited damage in the affected hemisphere, while after large lesions the contralesional side appears to vicariate the lost functions.
source: This variability in outcome may depend on the extent of damage: interhemispheric competition dominates in patients with limited damage in the affected hemisphere, while after large lesions the contralesional side appears to vicariate the lost functions (Bradnam et al., 2012; Di Pino et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by cited literature (Bradnam et al., 2012; Di Pino et al., 2014).

claim: The marked similarities in kinematic parameters of skilled reaching between humans and rodents indicates that mice can be used in pre-clinical studies with excellent translation potential.
source: Indeed, the marked similarities in kinematic parameters of skilled reaching between humans and rodents indicates that mice can be used in pre-clinical studies with excellent translation potential (Klein et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by cited literature (Klein et al., 2012).

claim: Unlike primates and humans, rodents do not have direct cortico-motoneuronal connections as the fastest pyramidal connections are dysinaptic.
source: On the other hand, it should be noted that, unlike primates and humans, rodents do not have direct cortico-motoneuronal connections as the fastest pyramidal connections are dysinaptic (Alstermark and Ogawa, 2004; Alstermark and Pettersson, 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by cited literature (Alstermark and Ogawa, 2004; Alstermark and Pettersson, 2014).

claim: The combined treatment of robotic training and contralesional hemisphere inactivation yields better results than the separate therapies.
source: Altogether, these data indicate that the combined treatment yields better results that the separate therapies.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the behavioral data comparing different treatment groups shown in Figure 7.

claim: The combined treatment promotes 'true' recovery of motor function, defined as the restoration of pre-lesion movement patterns.
source: In this manuscript, we define a rehabilitation protocol to promote 'true' recovery of motor function (i.e., the restoration of pre-lesion movement patterns) after focal cortical stroke in mice (Lai et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by kinematic data showing restoration of pre-lesion movement patterns and cited literature (Lai et al., 2015).

claim: The combined treatment normalizes transcallosal inhibition.
source: Such combined treatment normalized transcallosal inhibition and promoted recovery in general motor tests and in manual dexterity (i.e. skilled reaching) with a remarkable restoration of pre-lesion movement patterns.
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 10.

claim: The combined treatment promotes recovery in general motor tests and in manual dexterity with a remarkable restoration of pre-lesion movement patterns.
source: Such combined treatment normalized transcallosal inhibition and promoted recovery in general motor tests and in manual dexterity (i.e. skilled reaching) with a remarkable restoration of pre-lesion movement patterns.
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral and kinematic data shown in Figures 6, 7, and 8.

claim: The corpus callosum consists almost entirely of excitatory fibres.
source: These data are consistent with neuroanatomical observations indicating that the corpus callosum consists almost entirely of excitatory fibres, which implies that interhemispheric inhibition arises from the activation of local interneurons (Palmer et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by cited literature (Palmer et al., 2012).

claim: Interhemispheric inhibition arises from the activation of local interneurons.
source: These data are consistent with neuroanatomical observations indicating that the corpus callosum consists almost entirely of excitatory fibres, which implies that interhemispheric inhibition arises from the activation of local interneurons (Palmer et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by cited literature (Palmer et al., 2012) and the experimental data.

claim: Transcallosal neurons provide interhemispheric inhibition over the target hemisphere by contacting local interneurons, such as neurogliaform (NGF) cells in layer I.
source: It is well established that transcallosal neurons provide interhemispheric inhibition over the target hemisphere by contacting local interneurons, such as neurogliaform (NGF) cells in layer I.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge in the field.

claim: NGF cells exert GABAergic inhibitory effects over the dendrites of layer V pyramidal neurons, as demonstrated in somatosensory cortex.
source: NGF cells are known to exert GABAergic inhibitory effects over the dendrites of layer V pyramidal neurons, as demonstrated in somatosensory cortex (Palmer et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by cited literature (Palmer et al., 2012).

claim: Previous studies have shown a robust and early upregulation of GABA-B receptors in peri-infarct areas which suggest augmented responsiveness to GABA release.
source: In keeping with this idea, previous studies have shown a robust and early upregulation of GABA-B receptors in peri-infarct areas which suggest augmented responsiveness to GABA release (Que et al., 1999).
evidence: The claim is supported by cited literature (Que et al., 1999).

claim: Silencing of the contralesional motor area stimulates plastic reorganization in perilesional tissue, but the enhancement of plasticity without the guide of an appropriate motor rehabilitation regime is not sufficient to achieve a complete recovery.
source: One interpretation is that silencing of the contralesional motor area stimulates plastic reorganization in perilesional tissue, but the enhancement of plasticity without the guide of an appropriate motor rehabilitation regime is not sufficient to achieve a complete recovery (García-Alías et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the BoNT-only treatment results and is supported by cited literature (García-Alías et al., 2009).

claim: Robotic therapy is at least as effective as intensive conventional rehabilitation to improve motor functions, even in chronic patients with moderate-to-severe paresis.
source: The latest randomized studies have demonstrated that robotic therapy is at least as effective as intensive conventional rehabilitation to improve motor functions, even in chronic patients with moderate-to-severe paresis (Klamroth-Marganska et al., 2014)
evidence: The claim is supported by cited literature (Klamroth-Marganska et al., 2014).

claim: Robotic therapy is successfully used in low- and middle-income countries thanks to its advantages relative to costs and amount of work.
source: and thanks to its advantages relative to costs and amount of work it is successfully used also in low- and middle-income countries (Wagner et al., 2011; Bustamante Valles et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by cited literature (Wagner et al., 2011; Bustamante Valles et al., 2016).

claim: The M-Platform is a mechatronic device for mouse forelimb training that mimics a robot for upper limb rehabilitation in humans, the 'Arm-Guide'.
source: Here we employed the M-Platform, a mechatronic device for mouse forelimb training (Spalletti et al., 2014) that mimics a robot for upper limb rehabilitation in humans, the 'Arm-Guide' (Reinkensmeyer et al., 2000).
evidence: The claim is supported by cited literature (Spalletti et al., 2014; Reinkensmeyer et al., 2000).

claim: Clinical literature shows only task-specific improvements with little generalization after robotic training.
source: This is consistent with previous results in clinical literature, showing only task-specific improvements with little generalization after robotic training (Kwakkel et al., 2008; Panarese et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by cited literature (Kwakkel et al., 2008; Panarese et al., 2012).

claim: Timing of therapeutic treatments is critical for functional post-stroke outcome.
source: Timing of the therapeutic treatments is known to be critical for functional post-stroke outcome (Wahl et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by cited literature (Wahl et al., 2014).

claim: Early exercise may exacerbate brain injury, via excitotoxicity and generation of reactive oxygen species.
source: For robotic training, we chose to start the physiotherapy at day 5, since it is known that early exercise may exacerbate brain injury, via excitotoxicity and generation of reactive oxygen species (Kozlowski et al., 1996; Li et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by cited literature (Kozlowski et al., 1996; Li et al., 2017).

claim: Priming the brain with a 'plasticity-stimulating' treatment before the beginning of a rehabilitative treatment improves motor performance after brain lesions.
source: Moreover, it is widely believed that priming the brain with a 'plasticity-stimulating' treatment before the beginning of a rehabilitative treatment improves motor performance after brain lesions (Schäbitz et al., 2004; Starkey et al., 2012; Wahl et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by cited literature (Schäbitz et al., 2004; Starkey et al., 2012; Wahl et al., 2014).

claim: Spontaneous post-stroke amelioration occurs in the percentage of exact reachings but not in the kinematic parameters of movement.
source: We already demonstrated a spontaneous post-stroke amelioration in the percentage of exact reachings but not in the kinematic parameters of movement extracted by a custom-made algorithm (Lai et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by cited literature (Lai et al., 2015).

claim: Spontaneous recovery results clearly point to the development of compensatory motor strategies during post-stroke evolution.
source: These results clearly point to the development of compensatory motor strategies during post-stroke evolution (Caleo, 2015).
evidence: The claim is an interpretation supported by cited literature (Caleo, 2015).

claim: Reduction of GABAergic markers has been associated with improved motor outcomes triggered by motor rehabilitation.
source: Reduction of these markers has already been associated with improved motor outcomes triggered by motor rehabilitation (Zeiler et al., 2013)
evidence: The claim is supported by cited literature (Zeiler et al., 2013).

claim: Reduction of GABAergic markers is associated with the reopening of cortical plasticity that allows network reorganization and restoration of motor function.
source: and to the reopening of cortical plasticity that allows network reorganization and restoration of motor function (Ng et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by cited literature (Ng et al., 2015).

claim: Coupling physical rehabilitation with non-invasive brain stimulation (NIBS) techniques has been amply exploited in clinical practice.
source: Coupling physical rehabilitation with non-invasive brain stimulation (NIBS) techniques has been amply exploited in the clinical practice (Allman et al., 2016; Straudi et al., 2016; Yozbatiran et al., 2016; Chisari et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by cited literature (Allman et al., 2016; Straudi et al., 2016; Yozbatiran et al., 2016; Chisari et al., 2014).

claim: Studies in patients have highlighted a significant but generally small effect of physical rehabilitation combined with inhibitory NIBS applied to the contralesional cortex.
source: Studies in patients have highlighted a significant but generally small effect of physical rehabilitation combined with inhibitory NIBS applied to the contralesional cortex (Lefaucheur et al., 2014; Tedesco Triccas et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by cited literature (Lefaucheur et al., 2014; Tedesco Triccas et al., 2016).

claim: In humans, the kinematic analysis of skilled reaching is used in clinical practice to provide objective and quantitative information about forelimb motor function after injury.
source: In humans, the kinematic analysis of skilled reaching is used in clinical practice to provide objective and quantitative information about forelimb motor function after injury.
evidence: The claim is based on established clinical practice.

claim: ArcLen, Mean Speed and Smoothness parameters extracted from kinematic analysis show important similarities with observed trajectories in stroke patients.
source: Indeed, ArcLen, Mean Speed and Smoothness parameters extracted from our analysis show important similarities with observed trajectories in stroke patients (Cirstea and Levin, 2000; Panarese et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by cited literature (Cirstea and Levin, 2000; Panarese et al., 2012).

claim: The combined treatment of robotic training and contralesional hemisphere inactivation is highly effective in obtaining a complete 'true recovery' of motor function.
source: Overall, in this manuscript we have defined a rehabilitative protocol that is highly effective in obtaining a complete 'true recovery' (Zeiler and Krakauer, 2013; Reinkensmeyer et al., 2016) of motor function.
evidence: The claim is supported by the experimental data and cited literature (Zeiler and Krakauer, 2013; Reinkensmeyer et al., 2016).

claim: The results point to a synergistic effect of contralesional activity downregulation and robotic training after small ischemic infarcts in motor cortex.
source: The results point to a synergistic effect of contralesional activity downregulation and robotic training after small ischemic infarcts in motor cortex.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the combined treatment results.

claim: The contralesional cortex exerts an enhanced interhemispheric inhibition over the perilesional tissue after focal cortical stroke in mouse forelimb motor cortex.
source: Here, we demonstrate that the contralesional cortex exerts an enhanced interhemispheric inhibition over the perilesional tissue after focal cortical stroke in mouse forelimb motor cortex.
evidence: The claim is supported by the electrophysiological data presented in Figures 1-3.

claim: A rehabilitation protocol combining intensive, repeatable exercises on a robotic platform with reversible inactivation of the contralesional cortex promoted recovery in general motor tests and in manual dexterity.
source: Accordingly, we designed a rehabilitation protocol combining intensive, repeatable exercises on a robotic platform with reversible inactivation of the contralesional cortex. This treatment promoted recovery in general motor tests and in manual dexterity with remarkable restoration of pre-lesion movement patterns, evaluated by kinematic analysis.
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral and kinematic data presented in Figures 6-8.

claim: Recovery was accompanied by a reduction of transcallosal inhibition and 'plasticity brakes' over the perilesional tissue.
source: Recovery was accompanied by a reduction of transcallosal inhibition and 'plasticity brakes' over the perilesional tissue.
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological data in Figure 10 and immunohistochemical data in Figure 9.
